props.title: An Unmarried Woman

sections.content: An Unmarried Woman (1978) revolutionized Hollywood's portrayal of female independence during divorce. Jill Clayburgh's raw, vulnerable performance as Erica captured the messy reality of rebuilding life after a 16-year marriage implodes. Paul Mazursky's direction avoided melodrama, instead showing the gradual awakening of a woman discovering her identity beyond wife and mother. The film hit during peak feminist consciousness-raising, alongside Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore (1974) and Kramer vs. Kramer (1979), marking a shift from the neat happy endings of classic Hollywood divorce tales like The Awful Truth (1937). Starting Over|1979|Burt Reynolds and Jill Clayburgh star in this companion piece about divorce from the male perspective|Prime Video Three Women|1977|Robert Altman's dreamy exploration of female identity and friendship in the American Southwest|Criterion An Unmarried Woman|1978|A Manhattan woman rebuilds her life after her husband leaves her for a younger woman|Criterion

Mazursky's unflinching camera captures New York City as both prison and playground for newly single women. The film's groundbreaking therapy scenes normalized mental health support, while Erica's sexual reawakening challenged traditional "fallen woman" narratives. Her ultimate choice of independence over another marriage was radical for 1978, influencing later films like Waiting to Exhale (1995) and Under the Tuscan Sun (2003).

The film's visual style merges documentary realism with carefully composed frames that emphasize Erica's isolation and eventual liberation. Like contemporaries Opening Night (1977) and A Woman Under the Influence (1974), it uses extended takes and naturalistic dialogue to create psychological intimacy. The Manhattan locations, from SoHo galleries to Upper East Side apartments, become characters themselves, charting Erica's emotional geography. Opening Night|1977|Gena Rowlands stars as an actress confronting aging and identity|HBO Max Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore|1974|Ellen Burstyn won an Oscar as a widow starting over as a singer|TCM Kramer vs. Kramer|1979|Dustin Hoffman and Meryl Streep in a landmark divorce drama|Netflix SUBHEAD: Influence on Modern Cinema

An Unmarried Woman's DNA appears in countless modern divorce narratives, from Marriage Story (2019) to Blue Jasmine (2013). Its influence extends beyond divorce stories to any film about women's self-discovery, like Nomadland (2020) or Wild (2014). The film's greatest legacy may be its insistence that a woman's story doesn't end with marriage's dissolution - it often begins there.
